correctness.summary: Loop guard 'i * i <= n' overflows long for n near long.MaxValue. When i exceeds sqrt(n), i*i can wrap to a negative value, which is <= n, so the loop never terminates as intended and writes divisors out of the caller's buffer (out-of-bounds / never-ending growth).
correctness.triggeringInput: Divisors.Run(long.MaxValue, divs). At i=3037000500, i*i overflows to -9223372036709301616, and (-9223372036709301616 <= long.MaxValue) is true, so the loop continues past sqrt(n) writing beyond the intended divisor count (OOB writes / runaway).
correctness.rootCause: i*i is computed as a long multiplication with no overflow guard; for n > (long)sqrt(long.MaxValue)^2 region the product wraps negative and the comparison i*i <= n stays true forever.
correctness.suggestedFix: Use 'i <= n / i' as the loop guard instead of 'i * i <= n', or cap i with a precomputed integer sqrt(n) and compare i*i only when safe.

perf.summary: Hoist redundant divisions and the i*i loop bound to cut per-iteration work in the O(sqrt n) trial loop.
perf.currentCost: Each iteration computes i*i for the loop condition, then on a hit computes n/i twice (once for the != check, once to store). For composite-heavy n the division n/i is the dominant cost and is duplicated.
perf.proposedChange: Compute long q = n / i once per hit and reuse: 'if (n % i == 0) { divs[count++] = i; if (i != q) divs[count++] = q; }'. Optionally replace 'i*i <= n' with comparing i against a precomputed limit, but the simplest sure win is the single division. Combine the n%i and n/i via the fact that a hit already implies divisibility, so q = n/i is exact.
perf.rationale: 64-bit integer division is ~20-40 cycles on mobile ARM and is not pipelined well; halving divisions on every divisor hit is a real constant-factor win. i*i is cheaper than a div but still recomputed every loop.
perf.risk: Pure refactor, identical outputs. n>0 guaranteed by the early return so no div-by-zero. No overflow change (i*i already present in original).

perf.summary: Replace the O(d^2) insertion sort with an O(d) two-pointer merge exploiting the already-ordered halves produced by Run.
perf.currentCost: Run appends divisors as (i ascending) interleaved with (n/i descending): the small divisors 1,2,... are written in increasing order and the cofactors n/i are written in decreasing order. The final insertion Sort is O(d^2) on a buffer that is already two sorted runs.
perf.proposedChange: Have Run write small divisors into the front (ascending) and large divisors from the back of the buffer (which yields ascending when read back-to-front), then do a single in-place merge of the two contiguous sorted runs into ascending order in O(d). For a perfect square the middle element is written once. This removes Sort entirely.
perf.rationale: d (the divisor count) can be large for highly composite n (e.g. thousands). Insertion sort is quadratic in d; the merge is linear, turning a worst-case O(d^2) tail into O(d) with no extra allocation.
perf.risk: Must handle the perfect-square case (i == n/i) so the pivot element is not double-counted; the two runs meet in the middle. Output ordering must remain strictly ascending to preserve observable behavior. Needs care that the back-filled region and front region do not overlap before merge (they won't: total writes == count <= buffer size by contract).
